title: Diversity patterns in terrestrial tetrapod clades are governed by equilibrium dynamics
experiments_summary: The study analyzed species richness patterns across terrestrial tetrapods (amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals) using the following methods and analytical steps: (1) Species richness was mapped across equal-area grid cells (~110 km resolution) using range maps from existing databases, summing species whose ranges overlapped each cell. (2) Phylogenies for each tetrapod group were obtained from published sources; posterior distributions of trees (n=2,000) were sampled, and maximum-clade credibility (MCC) topologies were computed. (3) Clades were delineated using the Laplacian spectrum approach, a graph-theoretic method that clusters spectral density profiles of phylogenetic trees via k-means clustering (50 initial modalities), retaining only clades with ≥50 species, yielding 129 non-nested clades across the four groups. (4) Environmental predictors—mean annual temperature, mean annual precipitation, and net primary productivity (NPP)—were extracted for each grid cell from WorldClim and MODIS datasets. (5) Assemblage age (evolutionary time) was estimated using biogeographic region delineation based on phylogenetic turnover (evoregions), followed by ancestral range reconstruction using the DEC model in BioGeoBEARS, and calculation of mean lineage arrival times per grid cell using the 'Herodotools' package. (6) Speciation rates were quantified using three methods: the DR statistic, BAMM (run with four MCMC chains of 10 million generations each), and ClaDS; tip-based speciation rates were aggregated as median values per grid cell. DR was used as the primary metric for downstream analyses. (7) Structural equation models (SEMs) were fitted separately for each clade using the 'lavaan' R package, estimating direct and indirect effects of evolutionary time, speciation rates, temperature, precipitation, and productivity on species richness. Three indirect pathway classes were modeled: climate effects mediated through speciation rates, through evolutionary time, and through productivity. Model fit was assessed with CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR. (8) Four reduced, scenario-specific SEMs (Stable persistence, Speciation balance, Historical legacy, Cradles of diversity) were fitted per clade and compared using AIC and BIC to assess relative scenario support. (9) Linear regressions were fitted to test whether SEM-derived path coefficients varied systematically with clade-level traits: thermal physiology (endo- vs. ectothermy), clade age, species diversity, and geographic extent. (10) Spatial autocorrelation was assessed via Moran's I on SEM residuals, and sensitivity was evaluated by re-fitting all SEMs with latitude and longitude as additional predictors. (11) Sensitivity analyses included varying Laplacian modalities (40, 50, 60), excluding paraphyletic clades, using molecular-only phylogenies, substituting MPD and MBL as alternative evolutionary time metrics, and comparing DR, BAMM, and ClaDS speciation rate estimates.
